strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: replacing the redundant forward dynamics model (FDM) in the standard two-stage latent action modeling paradigm with the world model itself, allowing synergistic co-evolution of latent actions and world modeling.

Careful diagnostic and practical solution: the paper clearly identifies the representational collapse occurring during naive joint training (Figure 2) and resolves it using a simple yet effective frozen-world-model warm-up phase.

Comprehensive empirical validation: the approach is evaluated on video prediction metrics (FVD, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) across multiple datasets (OXE, EgoCentric, AgiBot, LIBERO), real-action adaptation, and downstream model predictive control (VP2 RoboDesk benchmark).

Solid ablations and scaling analysis: the submission provides insightful analyses on codebook health, scaling with respect to DiT model size and batch size, computational efficiency (wall-clock comparison in Appendix D.5), and generalization to an alternative backbone (Wan2.1).
weaknesses: The linear probing improvements on real-action recovery (Table 5) are quite subtle across most benchmarks, suggesting that the raw information content of the latent action space alone is not drastically different before downstream adaptation.

Joint training incurs noticeable computational overhead per step because gradients must propagate through a large 1.2B diffusion transformer to update the latent action model even during the warm-up phase, making training resource-intensive.

The warm-up duration selection is largely heuristic based on monitoring codebook utilization curves (e.g., 8k steps for OpenSora, 5k for Wan2.1); the paper lacks an automatic stopping criterion or formal guidelines for determining warm-up length across arbitrary backbones.

The investigation is confined strictly to discrete vector-quantized (VQ) action bottlenecks, leaving open the question of how co-evolution behaves with continuous or diffusion-based latent action formulations.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: eliminating the redundancy of the two-stage paradigm (IDM-FDM pretraining followed by separate world model training) in latent-action-based video world models.

Provides a insightful empirical diagnosis of why naive end-to-end joint training fails (codebook collapse caused by the strong pretrained video prior ignoring unaligned random/initial action signals), supported by clear codebook dynamics metrics (Figure 2).
Proposes a simple, elegant, and effective warm-up strategy (freezing the world model while propagating gradients to the IDM and conditioning layers) before transitioning to end-to-end co-evolution.

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple fronts: latent-action video generation fidelity across four diverse datasets, bidirectional co-evolution ablation studies, real-action adaptation, and downstream model-predictive control planning on the VP2 benchmark.

In-depth analysis of representation robustness (Figure 5), revealing why two-stage models fail under downstream adapter distribution shifts (collapsing to shortcuts) while joint co-evolution retains codebook entropy and utilization.
Demonstrates framework universality and scalability across different model capacities, training scales, and video generative backbones (both OpenSora and Wan2.1).
weaknesses: Linear probing metrics on real action recovery (Table 5) show only marginal differences between the two-stage baseline and CoLA-World, although downstream planning and adaptation benchmarks demonstrate clearer performance separation.

Backpropagating gradients through a large diffusion transformer back into the IDM introduces non-trivial per-step computational overhead compared to training a lightweight forward dynamics model, requiring significant GPU resources (8x H200 GPUs).

On several intricate manipulation tasks in the VP2 visual planning benchmark (e.g., Push Slide, Push Drawer, Flat Block in Table 4), absolute success rates remain quite low across all compared methods, illustrating existing limitations of visual MPC for contact-rich precision control.

The required warm-up length appears to vary depending on the backbone and batch size (e.g., 8k steps for OpenSora vs. 5k steps for Wan2.1, and 8k-15k across batch sizes in Table 6); more formal guidance or automatic criteria for determining the transition point would improve practical usability.

strengths: Compelling motivation and clear conceptual advance: The paper tackles an important open problem in latent action world models—moving beyond the redundant, decoupled two-stage paradigm (IDM-FDM followed by a frozen latent world model) to a unified end-to-end co-evolution framework.

Insightful failure diagnosis and simple, effective solution: The manuscript provides a clear empirical explanation of why naive joint training of a from-scratch IDM and a pretrained video diffusion model causes catastrophic representation collapse in the VQ codebook (Figure 2), and demonstrates that a frozen-WM warmup phase cleanly resolves this alignment bottleneck (Figure 3).

Thorough experimental validation: The method is evaluated comprehensively across multiple dimensions—action linear probing, action-conditioned video generation quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FVD across OXE, EgoCentric, AgiBot, and LIBERO), real-action adaptation via MLP adapters, and closed-loop visual planning on the VP² RoboDesk benchmark.

Strong mechanistic analysis: Ablations in Section 4.3 (Figure 4) cleanly dissect the bidirectional benefits (the world model providing evolving, causally informative gradients as a tutor, and the evolving LAM providing an adaptable interface), and Figure 5 offers an insightful diagnostic into why the two-stage approach collapses under out-of-distribution downstream adaptation.

Good generality and scalability checks: The authors validate the framework across varying model sizes (Figure 6), batch sizes (Table 6), and successfully reproduce the gains on an entirely different video backbone, Wan2.1 (Table 7).
weaknesses: Tight coupling to discrete vector quantization (VQ): The collapse analysis and the warmup remedy are studied exclusively within a discrete VQ latent action space. It is unclear whether continuous latent action formulations (e.g., Gaussian VAEs or flow-based latents) suffer from the same representational collapse or whether continuous latents would behave more stably without requiring such warmup.

Computational overhead of end-to-end backpropagation: Backpropagating flow matching gradients through a 1.2B+ parameter DiT into the IDM is computationally demanding (6s/step vs. 3.6s/step for standard IDM/FDM training, as noted in Table 8). While wall-clock time comparisons to matched performance levels are provided, this training cost remains non-trivial.

Marginal differences on static representation probing: In Table 5, the linear probing losses across several robotic datasets show very small differences between the 2-stage baseline and CoLA-World (e.g., 0.0827 vs. 0.0815 on Bridge; 0.1614 vs. 0.1623 on Libero), meaning static probing alone does not capture the claimed representational advantages, forcing the argument to rely primarily on generative and planning metrics.

Modest absolute success rates in visual planning: While CoLA-World significantly outperforms AdaWorld and the 2-stage baseline on RoboDesk (Table 3 and Table 4), the absolute success rates on several manipulation tasks remain below 10% (e.g., Push Slide, Push Drawer, Flat Block), illustrating the ongoing difficulty of using video diffusion world models for precision manipulation control.
